# Rooting out bias

## Authors

- Bridget M Kuehn<sup>1</sup> ([ORCID: 0000-0001-8783-4419](https://orcid.org/0000-0001-8783-4419)) †

### Affiliations

1. eLife Chicago United States

† Corresponding author

## Abstract

Tackling unconscious bias is a major challenge for journals and the rest of the scientific community.

## Underrepresentation is widespread

Neef's study is one of many across a variety of disciplines to document the underrepresentation of women in peer-reviewed journals. An analysis of the 20 earth and space science journals published by the American Geophysical Union (AGU) between 2012 and 2016 found that 27% of first authors were women, and that 28% of AGU members were women: however, only 21% of reviewers were women (Lerback and Hanson, 2017). And a study of more than 200,000 papers published in five major astronomy journals between 1950 and 2015 found that women authors received 10% fewer citations (Caplar et al., 2017).

Although many of these studies were not designed to tease out the cause of this underrepresentation, they do point to potential clues. Neef and colleagues found that male and female editors had a tendency to select reviewers of the same gender: men were selected by male editors to review 73% of the time, and female editors selected women reviewers 33% of the time. The female-female preference was driven by a small number of female editors who chose women reviewers at a very high rate, says Neef.

A preference for like individuals is a common human trait, and is likely to extend to other areas like hiring, grant funding and promotions. "It’s a hard thing to fight because you are comfortable working with people who are like you," says Knezek. But if left unabated it could have detrimental effects on peer review and science more generally, by reducing the ability of women or other underrepresented groups to advance or stay in scientific careers.

Women scientists are also less likely to have their grants funded, as are scientists from certain minorities (Ginther et al., 2011). Patricia Devine of the University of Wisconsin-Madison and colleagues recently completed collecting data for a study on whether identical grant applications with names that are indicative of a white male, white female, black maleor black female will be graded differently by reviewers for the US National Institutes of Health (NIH). She hopes the study will be able to tease out whether the lower funding rates are caused by differences in quality or by bias, which will help the NIH develop interventions. "If scientists aren’t being treated equally because of their gender or race we will not be in a position to fund the very best scientists," says Devine. "That can threaten the integrity of the scientific literature."

Devine and her colleagues have also developed tools to help individuals and organizations identify and mitigate biases. These include exercises that help individuals recognize unconscious bias and help them to focus on an individual’s merits rather than their gender or race. To test this approach, they conducted a randomized trial at the University of Wisconsin that involved offering a workshop on the tools to faculty in some departments but not others (Carnes et al., 2015). After this intervention, faculty in departments who were offered the workshop were more likely to report taking action against bias than faculty in the control departments. "They are more tuned in and aware of their own proclivity for bias," says Devine. "When you are tuned in you can reach for a tool."

Both men and women faculty members in intervention departments reported greater satisfaction with their work environment. The hiring of women, which was about 32% in all departments prior to the trial, also increased by 15% in the intervention departments. "Men and women both felt that their work was more respected in intervention departments than control departments," says Devine. "They felt they could raise issues like family needs without being stigmatized." However, Devine stresses that this type of intervention can only address unconscious bias – it will not help to address overt bias, such as people who openly express the view that women are inferior in science.

## The way ahead

Making progress towards gender equality in peer review and science more generally will require a concerted effort on the part of journals, professional societies and individual scientists to root out bias. Neef suggests that all journals should conduct the type of analysis that he and his colleagues did, and recommends the use of pop-up reminders and other mechanisms to gently nudge the behavior of editors or reviewers. At the recent International Congress on Peer Review in Chicago Jory Lerback, formerly of the AGU, reported how asking authors to think of women and underrepresented groups when suggesting reviewers for their papers resulted in a statistically significant increase in the number of women reviewers suggested by male authors submitting to Geophysical Research Letters.

Professional organizations should also be looking at the representation of women and minorities as speakers, poster presenters and participants at scientific meetings, and setting up both formal and informal support networks for people from underrepresented groups at such meetings, says Knezek. And in addition to policing their own tendency for bias, she says it is important for scientists to speak up when they see bias, even if it is uncomfortable.

## Note

This Feature Article is part of a collection of articles on peer review.

results.result: Women are underrepresented as peer reviewers in earth and space science journals. Analysis of 20 AGU journals (2012-2016) found that while 27% of first authors and 28% of AGU members were women, only 21% of reviewers were women, demonstrating underrepresentation across multiple disciplines.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C4 provide specific quantitative data from a cited study (Lerback and Hanson, 2017) showing clear underrepresentation of women reviewers relative to their representation among authors and society members. C36 contextualizes this as part of a broader pattern across disciplines. The data are internally consistent and appropriately cited.

results.result: Women authors in astronomy receive fewer citations than their male counterparts. A study of over 200,000 papers in five major astronomy journals (1950-2015) found women authors received 10% fewer citations.
results.evaluation: Claim C5 is supported by a specific citation (Caplar et al., 2017) with clear quantitative data from a large sample size (>200,000 papers) over an extended time period. The finding is presented as a factual result from prior work with appropriate attribution.

results.result: Editors exhibit same-gender preference when selecting peer reviewers. Male editors selected male reviewers 73% of the time, while female editors selected female reviewers 33% of the time, with the female-female preference driven by a small number of female editors with very high selection rates.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C9 present specific quantitative findings from Neef and colleagues' study with clear percentages and an explanation for the observed pattern. The data demonstrate homophily in reviewer selection, though the asymmetry between male and female editor behavior is notable and explained by C9.

results.result: Women scientists and scientists from certain minorities experience lower grant funding rates. This disparity is documented in the literature and extends gender and racial bias beyond peer review to research funding.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C14 are supported by citation to Ginther et al., 2011, providing empirical evidence for funding disparities. The claims are appropriately scoped and attributed to prior work, though the manuscript does not provide the specific magnitude of the disparity.

results.result: A study is underway to determine whether bias affects NIH grant application reviews. The study uses identical applications with names indicating different race-gender combinations to distinguish between quality differences and bias as causes of lower funding rates.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C16 describe an ongoing study that has completed data collection but not analysis. Since results are not yet available, this represents planned work rather than a completed finding. The study design appears sound for addressing the research question, but no conclusions can be drawn yet.

results.result: A bias-reduction intervention involving workshops on recognizing unconscious bias improved outcomes in academic departments. A randomized trial at University of Wisconsin showed that intervention departments had faculty who reported taking more action against bias, greater work satisfaction, and a 15% increase in hiring of women (from 32% baseline).
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C27 describe a well-designed randomized controlled trial (Carnes et al., 2015) with multiple outcome measures showing consistent positive effects. The study includes appropriate controls, quantitative outcomes (C24-C25), and qualitative measures (C26-C27). The intervention's effectiveness is supported by converging evidence across behavioral, attitudinal, and hiring outcomes.

results.result: The bias-reduction intervention can only address unconscious bias and is ineffective against overt bias. The intervention is not designed to change the views of individuals who openly express beliefs about gender inferiority in science.
results.evaluation: Claim C28 appropriately identifies a limitation of the intervention based on its design and mechanism of action. This is a reasonable inference about scope, as interventions targeting awareness of unconscious bias would not be expected to address explicitly held discriminatory beliefs. The limitation is clearly stated by the intervention developers.

results.result: Prompting authors to consider women and underrepresented groups when suggesting reviewers increases diversity of reviewer suggestions. An intervention at Geophysical Research Letters resulted in a statistically significant increase in women reviewers suggested by male authors.
results.evaluation: Claim C32 reports a specific intervention with a statistically significant outcome presented at a peer review conference. The finding is appropriately scoped with clear attribution to Lerback. However, the magnitude of the effect and details of statistical testing are not provided, limiting full evaluation.

results.result: Homophily (preference for similar individuals) is a common human trait that likely extends to professional contexts including hiring, grant funding, and promotions. If unaddressed, this bias could harm peer review and science by limiting advancement opportunities for women and underrepresented groups.
results.evaluation: Claim C10 is supported by established psychological knowledge about homophily. Claims C11-C12 are logical inferences extending this principle to professional contexts, consistent with the empirical findings presented elsewhere in the manuscript (C6-C9, C13-C14). The reasoning is sound, though C12 is somewhat speculative about future consequences.

results.result: Unequal treatment based on gender or race in science undermines meritocracy and threatens scientific integrity. If bias prevents equal treatment, funding agencies cannot select the best scientists, potentially compromising the quality of scientific literature.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C18 present a logical argument about the consequences of bias for scientific quality and integrity. While somewhat speculative, the reasoning is sound: systematic bias in evaluation processes would by definition prevent purely merit-based selection. These are expert opinions from a researcher studying bias interventions.

results.result: Addressing gender bias in science requires multi-level interventions. Recommendations include journals conducting bias analyses and implementing nudges for editors/reviewers, professional organizations monitoring representation at meetings and creating support networks, and individual scientists speaking up against observed bias.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C35 present a coherent set of recommendations based on the evidence presented in the manuscript. The recommendations are appropriately scoped to different stakeholders and are logical extensions of the documented problems. C32 provides some empirical support for the effectiveness of nudge-based interventions.

results.result: Unconscious bias represents a major challenge for scientific publishing and the broader scientific community. While multiple studies document underrepresentation of women across disciplines, most were not designed to establish causation, though they provide clues about underlying mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C1 and C36-C38 provide appropriate framing for the manuscript. C36 is supported by multiple cited studies. C37 correctly identifies a limitation of observational studies, while C38 notes they still provide valuable insights. C1 is a reasonable synthesis given the evidence of widespread bias documented throughout the manuscript.
